questions.prompt: What is the defining property of a binary min-heap?

options.text: Every parent node is smaller than or equal to its child nodes.
options.explanation: In a min-heap, the root holds the smallest element and every parent is less than or equal to its children.

options.text: Every node has exactly two children with ascending integer values.
options.explanation: Heaps are not sorted left to right like binary search trees; only the parent-child relationship matters.

options.text: Left child values must always be strictly greater than right child values.
options.explanation: Binary heaps do not require any ordering relationship between sibling nodes.

options.text: All leaf nodes must contain negative floating-point numbers.
options.explanation: Binary heaps work with any comparable element type, positive or negative.

options.explanation: 2 * i applies to 1-indexed heap arrays, not 0-indexed arrays.

2 * i + 2 finds the right child of index i, not the left child.
(i - 1) / 2 finds the parent node index, not the left child.

questions.prompt: In a 0-indexed binary heap array, which formula computes the parent of an element at index i?

options.explanation: i / 2 is used in 1-indexed heaps; in 0-indexed heaps index 0 would yield invalid parent math.
2 * i - 1 does not compute the parent index in a binary heap.
Integer division (i - 1) / 2 correctly maps both left (2p + 1) and right (2p + 2) children back to parent p.
(i + 1) / 2 computes an incorrect forward index rather than the parent.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of extracting the minimum element from a binary min-heap with N elements?

options.explanation: Inspecting the minimum takes O(1), but removing it requires sifting down.

options.text: O(N)
options.explanation: O(N) is linear scan time; heaps do not scan all elements to extract.

options.text: O(N log N)
options.explanation: O(N log N) is the time to sort an entire array, not a single extraction.

options.text: O(log N)
options.explanation: Extracting the minimum swaps the last item to the root and sifts down at most the height of the tree, which is O(log N).

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity to inspect the root element using peek on a binary heap?

options.text: O(1) constant time, because the root always sits at array index zero.
options.explanation: The extreme element (min or max) is always stored at index 0, allowing instant access.

options.text: O(log N) time, because the root must be verified against leaf nodes.
options.explanation: No verification or tree traversal is needed to read index 0.

options.text: O(N) time, because all array elements must be scanned sequentially.
options.explanation: A full scan is only required in an unsorted array, not a heap.

options.text: O(N squared) time, because comparisons trigger an internal sort pass.
options.explanation: Peek does not mutate or sort the underlying collection.

questions.prompt: Why can a binary heap be stored in a contiguous array without using node pointers?

options.text: Because Swift arrays allocate recursive memory cells automatically.
options.explanation: Array memory is flat and contiguous, not recursive.

options.text: Because a heap is a complete binary tree with predictable child indices.
options.explanation: A complete binary tree has no gaps, so parent and child positions are computed directly with simple arithmetic.

options.text: Because every heap element must be a hashable 64-bit integer type.
options.explanation: Binary heaps support any comparable type, not just 64-bit integers.

options.text: Because Swift standard library dictionaries store heap links in memory.
options.explanation: A binary heap uses an array, not a dictionary or hash map.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity to build a binary heap from an unsorted array of N elements using bottom-up sift-down?

options.text: O(N squared)
options.explanation: O(N^2) would be worse than standard bubble sort.

options.text: O(N log N)
options.explanation: Repeatedly calling insert takes O(N log N), but bottom-up heapify runs in linear time.

options.text: O(N)
options.explanation: Bottom-up heapify takes O(N) because half the nodes are leaves requiring 0 swaps and higher levels have exponentially fewer nodes.

options.text: O(log N)
options.explanation: A sub-linear time is impossible because every element must be processed.

questions.prompt: Why is a min-heap of size K used instead of a max-heap to find the K largest elements in a stream?

options.text: The min-heap root holds the smallest of the top K, so smaller items can be discarded quickly.
options.explanation: Keeping a min-heap of size K bounds space to O(K). If a new number exceeds the root, replace it and sift down in O(log K) time.

options.text: A max-heap cannot accept more than K elements before throwing a runtime exception.
options.explanation: Max-heaps can hold any number of elements without runtime errors.

options.text: Swift language rules forbid reversing array order when comparing integers.
options.explanation: Swift supports custom comparators including greater-than closures.

options.text: Min-heaps store all stream elements inside a private secondary SQLite database.
options.explanation: Min-heaps operate purely in memory using standard array allocations.

questions.prompt: Where is a newly inserted element initially placed before sifting up in an array-backed binary heap?

options.text: At index zero, shifting all existing elements one position to the right.
options.explanation: Inserting at index 0 would require O(N) array shifting.

options.text: At the very end of the array, preserving the complete binary tree structure.
options.explanation: Appending to the end takes amortized O(1) time and preserves the complete tree shape before sifting up.

options.text: In the exact middle index of the array buffer.
options.explanation: Inserting in the middle violates the complete binary tree property.

options.text: Inside a temporary global cache outside the heap array.
options.explanation: The element is placed directly into the heap array.

questions.prompt: When deleting the root of a binary min-heap, which element replaces the root before sifting down begins?

options.text: The left child of the root node.
options.explanation: Promoting the left child leaves an empty hole in the tree.

options.text: The right child of the root node.
options.explanation: Promoting the right child leaves a gap and breaks tree completeness.

options.text: The last element in the array.
options.explanation: Moving the last element to index 0 preserves tree completeness, followed by sifting down to restore heap order.

options.text: The median value across all leaf nodes.
options.explanation: Finding the median across leaves would take O(N) time.

questions.prompt: What is a primary operational difference between a binary search tree (BST) and a binary heap?

options.text: A BST orders left child < parent < right child, while a heap only orders parent versus children.
options.explanation: A BST maintains total horizontal order across all keys, while a heap only maintains vertical parent-child priority.

options.text: A binary heap requires linked pointers while a BST must use contiguous flat arrays.
options.explanation: The opposite is true: heaps use arrays while BSTs typically use node pointers.

options.text: Searching for an arbitrary value takes O(1) in a heap and O(N squared) in a BST.
options.explanation: Searching an arbitrary value in a heap takes O(N) linear scan time.

options.text: Binary search trees only permit integer keys while binary heaps permit any type.
options.explanation: Both structures support any comparable data type.

questions.prompt: Which operation restores the heap property after appending a new element to the end of a binary heap?

options.text: Sift-down from the root to the leaf.
options.explanation: Sift-down is used when removing the root, not after appending to the leaf.

options.text: Sift-up from the newly appended leaf toward the root.
options.explanation: The newly appended item bubbles up by swapping with its parent until the heap property holds.

options.text: Rotating the binary tree using an AVL rebalance operation.
options.explanation: Binary heaps use sifting in arrays, not AVL tree rotations.

options.text: Reversing the entire underlying array.
options.explanation: Reversing an array does not restore heap order.

options.text: At either index 1 or index 2.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why a min-heap of size K is faster than sorting the entire array. Mention both time and space complexity.

rubric.criterion: Explains that sorting the entire array takes O(N log N) time and O(N) auxiliary space
Explains that a min-heap of size K takes O(N log K) time and O(K) space
Notes that smaller items can be discarded as soon as they are smaller than the min-heap root

questions.modelAnswer: Sorting an entire array of size N requires O(N log N) time and O(N) space. Using a min-heap of size K bounds auxiliary space to O(K) and runs in O(N log K) time. When K is much smaller than N, this saves significant memory and CPU time because numbers smaller than the heap root are discarded immediately.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain the difference between sift-up and sift-down in a binary heap. Identify which operation is triggered during insertion and which during extraction.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that sift-up is used after insertion at the array tail
Identifies that sift-down is used after extracting the root element
Describes movement direction (sift-up travels up toward parent, sift-down travels down comparing with children)

questions.modelAnswer: Sift-up is used during insertion when a new item is appended to the end of the heap array. It compares the element with its parent and bubbles up toward the root. Sift-down is used during root extraction when the last array element replaces the deleted root. It compares the element with both children and swaps downward with the smaller child until heap order is restored.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why building a binary heap using bottom-up sift-down takes O(N) time instead of O(N log N).

rubric.criterion: Explains that leaves make up roughly half the nodes (N / 2) and require zero sifting
Notes that higher levels require more sift work but contain exponentially fewer nodes
Mentions that repeated insertion takes O(N log N) because most nodes sift all the way up

questions.modelAnswer: Building a heap with bottom-up sift-down takes O(N) time because roughly half the nodes are leaves that require zero swaps. As you move up the tree, the maximum number of swaps increases linearly with height, but the number of nodes at each level decreases exponentially. The resulting mathematical summation converges to O(N), whereas repeated insertion takes O(N log N).

questions.modelAnswer: We maintain two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half of numbers and a min-heap for the larger half. We keep the two heaps balanced so their sizes differ by at most one element. To compute the median in O(1) time, read the root of the larger heap. Average the two roots when both sizes are equal.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare a binary heap with a binary search tree (BST). When would you choose a heap over a BST in an iOS application?

rubric.criterion: Compares heap (only vertical priority order) with BST (complete horizontal key order)
Notes heap storage advantage (flat array with cache locality and zero pointer overhead)
Identifies scenario: choose heap for priority queues / top K items; choose BST for arbitrary key search or range queries

questions.modelAnswer: A binary heap only maintains vertical parent-child priority, whereas a binary search tree maintains total order across all keys. A heap is stored in a flat array, providing excellent cache locality with zero pointer overhead. Choose a heap when you only need fast access to extreme values or priority scheduling. Choose a BST when you need arbitrary key lookups or ordered range searches.
